title: Embracing high clock frequency alongside complex design
decision: Opted to also embrace the speed-demon (high clock rate) approach while retaining complex high-IPC design elements.
alternatives_or_rejected: Traditional IBM UNIX systems in the 'braniac' camp (more complex design emphasizing higher instructions-per-cycle rather than high clock rate).
rationale: To maintain leadership position and deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies; the design was initially introduced at 1.1 GHz and 1.3 GHz, surpassing other 64-bit microprocessors in key benchmarks.
outcome: POWER4 achieved high frequencies while supporting superscalar out-of-order execution with high IPC potential (up to 8 issue, sustained 5 completion).

title: RAS philosophy beyond ECC and reliable parts
where_in_paper: Guiding principles (Leadership in reliability, availability, and serviceability)
decision: Required an approach that eliminated outages and provided redundancy where errors could not be eliminated; transform hard machine stops (checkstops) into synchronous machine interrupts to software where possible.
alternatives_or_rejected: Achieving high reliability only by choosing reliable parts and incorporating ECC logic into major arrays.
rationale: Servers have evolved toward continuous operation; outages of any kind are not tolerated; build on mainframe-like RAS attributes already being introduced.
outcome: Pervasive RAS design throughout the system (detailed further in companion paper); first-failure data capture, error detection/logging, and recovery mechanisms integrated.

title: Full-system co-design from the outset
decision: Began with the full design in mind up front; designed the entire system together from processor to memory and I/O bridge chips; processor designed to fit effectively in this environment.
alternatives_or_rejected: Designing the processor in isolation then later adding a subsystem (implied by emphasis on co-design necessity).
rationale: A new high-performance processor needs a new subsystem to feed it effectively; marriage of process technology, packaging, and microarchitecture to allow software to exploit them; optimize the system as a whole.
outcome: POWER4 defined as an architecture/technology for interconnecting chips into systems (not just a chip); distributed-switch interconnect for up to 32-way SMP; buses scale with processor frequency to preserve balance.

title: Single design for both technical and commercial workloads
where_in_paper: Guiding principles (Balanced technical and commercial performance)
decision: A single design addressing both high-performance computing (high-bandwidth) and commercial (data-sharing/SMP scaling) requirements, supporting both pSeries and iSeries.
alternatives_or_rejected: Separate designs optimized only for technical (like prior POWER3) or only for commercial (like prior RS64 family).
rationale: As e-business evolves, data-intensive demands merge with commercial requirements; need to satisfy both historical high-bandwidth HPC and SMP scaling; enable one design for what became pSeries and iSeries.
outcome: POWER4 addresses both commercial and technical requirements; binary-compatible 64-bit PowerPC extension used across systems.

title: Dual-core chip with shared L2 and scalable fabric interconnect
where_in_paper: POWER4 chip section and system interconnect discussion
decision: Two identical processors on one chip sharing a unified L2 via CIU crossbar; interconnect topology called distributed switch (new to industry) allowing up to 32-way SMP via chip-chip and MCM-MCM buses that scale with frequency.
alternatives_or_rejected: Treating POWER4 solely as a single-processor chip (explicitly rejected: 'cannot be considered only a chip'); fixed-frequency buses that would unbalance systems as frequencies rise.
rationale: SMP optimization for high-throughput multitasking; full-system design; preserve system balance as technology improves frequencies; leverage packaging (4 chips/module, 4 modules for 32-way).
outcome: 174M-transistor chip; 2-way SMP model to software per chip; scalable fabric supporting 8-way modules and 32-way systems; buses (except JTAG) scale proportionally with processor frequency.
